transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-30
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Nimbus CTO), Ben Torres (Nimbus SRE), Maya Gupta (Nimbus ML Engineer)

[00:00] Samira: All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check on audio — you can hear me?
[00:06] Aisha: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:08] Samira: Awesome. Agenda today: quick recap of the load test results Liam ran, talk sizing + autoscaling, burst/fallback behavior, then next steps.
[00:18] Liam: I'll share my screen real quick with the benchmark spreadsheet, just a sec. (screen share) Ok, so I ran two configs last night: a 2-node pool with A100-40g equiv and a 4-node pool. We ran sustained concurrency of 150 rps and 3x burst tests up to 450 rps.
[00:36] Maya: Quick q, is the 150 rps simulating per-route or aggregate?
[00:39] Liam: Aggregate across the service, that maps to about 1.2M tokens per minute in our test prompt shape.
[00:45] Ben: And what model variant were you using? The smaller fp16 or the quant?
[00:49] Liam: We used Redwood-optimized 13B fp16 baseline and then a 13B Q4 variant for the burst profile. Note there was some jitter in token time for the quant run - the transcriber here might say Q four but the numbers show increased variance.
[01:05] Samira: So headline: 2-node config met 50th pct latency SLO but 95th pct spiked around 1.2s which is above your target of 800ms, right?
[01:14] Aisha: Correct, our target is 800ms at 95th. That spike is in the tail we cared about.
[01:18] Liam: Right — on the 4-node pool 95th is down to ~700ms, headroom for bursts. Memory pressure during KV cache warmup added about 150ms for first requests. There's a KV cahce warmup which is expected.
[01:35] Ben: KV cahce? do you mean KV cache?
[01:37] Liam: Yeah sorry, K V cache — my typo.
[01:39] Maya: That warmup is a concern for our first-time-invokes from new tenants. Is there an approach to pre-warm?
[01:44] Liam: Two options — proactive prefix caching on the pool for common prompt prefixes, or keep a small reserved 'hot' subset of nodes that never scale down below 1 node to preserve warmed KV state.
[01:55] Samira: For Dedicated we usually recommend a small warm pool sized to expected cold-start rate plus an autoscale policy with cooldowns. Example: min_capacity 1 node, scale_step 1 node, scale_up_threshold 70% CPU or 60% token queue for 30s, cooldown 90s. That lets you absorb brief spikes without overscaling.
[02:13] Aisha: Can you clarify token queue based scaling? We don't have a token queue metric today.
[02:18] Liam: Token queue is a Redwood metric that approximates outstanding tokens being processed — helps with tail behavior. If we don't have that in your infra, we can use GPU utilization + request latency as a proxy.
[02:28] Ben: For our security review we need guaranteed isolation and that reserved nodes won't be shared with other customers.
[02:33] Samira: Dedicated pools are fully isolated — reserved capacity is tenant-dedicated. We'll add the dedicated SLA language to the docs we send.
[02:40] Maya: Back to burst — you mentioned fallback to smaller model variants. How seamless is that?
[02:44] Liam: We do model routing by policy. On a high-queue condition the router can fall back to a compatible quantized 13B or a 7B variant with a configurable quality budget. There's some scoring difference but we can guarantee latency SLOs. Note: Quality regression tests should be added to your eval suite.
[03:00] Aisha: We care about ROI — if we keep min_capacity >0 for warm nodes that increases costs. Can you quantify delta?
[03:06] Samira: Rough back-of-envelope: keeping one A100-equivalent node up 24/7 is about X in monthly committed cost; we will send concrete SKUs and committed vs burst pricing. For many customers the cost of one warm node is cheaper than frequent cold-start penalties in user experience.
[03:20] Ben: What's the autoscaler cooldown impact if we set cooldown to 30s vs 90s?
[03:24] Liam: Shorter cooldown reacts faster to bursts but increases oscillation risk and can overscale if traffic is spiky. 90s is our default tradeoff for stability; you can do shorter for more aggressive latency SLOs but expect higher cost.
[03:36] Maya: Any guidance on node sizes — we deploy on A100-80g and A10g clouds; which maps better?
[03:41] Liam: For inference-heavy 13B models A100-40/80 is preferred; A10 gives lower cost but you'll need more nodes and might lose a bit on 95th tail. We'll include perf numbers per GPU type in the doc.
[03:52] Samira: Also consider batching: continuous batching can reduce per-token cost significantly but increases tail for single-user low-latency calls. If you have a mix, we recommend per-route policies.
[04:05] Aisha: Can Redwood autoscale by route? We want chat endpoints to have tighter SLOs than async generation.
[04:09] Samira: Yes, you can configure per-route model selection and per-route autoscale thresholds in Dedicated.
[04:14] Ben: For the burst tests you did, what recovery time did you observe once traffic dropped?
[04:18] Liam: In the 4-node run scaling down to 2 nodes took about 3 minutes with default cooldowns. With a smaller cooldown it can be faster but then you risk thrashing.
[04:26] Maya: Another practical question — what about preemptible spot GPUs for burst?
[04:30] Liam: We support burst pools that can include spot capacity; the router can failover to spot when on-demand is saturated but spots can be reclaimed — we recommend a mixed-strategy: keep at least 1 on-demand warm node and allow spots for additional burst capacity.
[04:43] Aisha: Security quick check — does Dedicated expose audit logs and KMS integration?
[04:48] Samira: Yes, audit logs, SAML/SSO, and KMS integration are supported. We'll send the SOC2 + KMS integration docs after the call.
[04:56] Ben: Great. On the benchmark, can we get the raw latency distributions? We're especially interested in 99th pct.
[05:02] Liam: Sure, I'll upload histograms and 50/95/99 percentiles to the shared folder.
[05:07] Maya: For model fallback, will the API signal the variant to the app? We want to display a small note if model downgraded for quality transparency.
[05:13] Samira: Yes, the response metadata includes model_variant and a reason code when fallback occurs; you can surface that to users.
[05:20] Aisha: Nice. Any blocker items from Redwood side to run the 95th pct run?
[05:24] Liam: We need your traffic histogram and expected concurrency windows. Also confirm which GPU family to test (A100 vs A10).
[05:31] Aisha: We'll send that by tomorrow.
[05:33] Samira: Cool. Let's recap next steps.
[05:36] Speaker 2: (unclear) recap?
[05:38] Samira: Recap: Redwood run detailed 95th/99th runs on 2x and 4x node configs; share pricing + SKU sheet; provide autoscaler policy template; Nimbus to send traffic histogram and security contact. We'll meet next week for an autoscaler deep dive.
[05:53] Ben: Sounds good, thanks.
[05:55] Maya: One last question, for the KV cahce warmup, is there a warmup API to pre-populate?
[06:00] Liam: We have an internal prewarm endpoint in Private workflows; for Dedicated we can provide a prewarm script you can run as part of deployment — will include sample.
[06:09] Aisha: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[06:11] Samira: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[06:14] (call ends)

Notes: occasional transcription typos (KV cahce, autscaling) preserved. References: shared spreadsheet link (link://redwood/poc-benchmarks-987), pricing doc (link://redwood/dedicated-skus), SOC2 package (link://redwood/security/soc2-package).
